issues.author: ericscheffler
issues.body:
### Check for previous/existing GitHub issues

- [x] I have checked for previous/existing GitHub issues

### Issue Type?

Feature Request

### Description

I have my AVM CI/CD environment configured to use an internal Azure subscription; there are Azure policies that will prevent deployment of Storage Accounts with public access, and Event Hub Namespaces without Local Authentication disabled:

- Storage Account - Requires either publicNetworkAccess disabled or a skip tag
- Event Hub Namespace - Requires disableLocalAuth set to true or a skip tag

To work around this the policy managers have enabled the use of skip tags; Azure tags with specific values can be added to resources to allow them to be deployed normally. The problem is that  diagnostic.dependencies.bicep does not have the tags parameter exposed, so the necessary skip tags can't be added to allow my tests to complete without being impeded by policy. 

Propose the following:

- Add the 'tags' parameter to the resources defined in diagnostic.dependencies.bicep, and expose the parameter as an input
- Consider disabling public access for these resources altogether if not needed for any other patterns or resources
- API updates as appropriate

comments_list.author: AlexanderSehr
comments_list.body:
Hey @ericscheffler,
Thanks for the issue. @eriqua please also take a look at this when you have the chance. Eric and I already chatted about it in the last few weeks. 🙂

comments_list.author: eriqua
comments_list.body:
@ericscheffler @AlexanderSehr I wouldn't see any problem in exposing tags. I believe this would cover already, likely the easiest fix and I'd tend to start with that. 
In a second stage, even extend the same to all dependencies for the same reason. For example, I'd expect dependency subnets not having nsg could be an issue for test environments protected by policies.
As per disabling public access I guess this would come together with adding private endpoints, so maybe we can discuss this a little further. Dependencies are usually implemented as minimum required resources, we also skip psrule on those as the primary goal of the test is to validate the primary resource. I believe adding tags can be a good trade off.
The only downside we faced with tags is they contribute to the number of write operations, increasing the chance of throttling. In our case I don't expect them to have an impact in this sense though.

comments_list.author: ericscheffler
comments_list.body:
@eriqua 
> For example, I'd expect dependency subnets not having nsg could be an issue for test environments protected by policies

This is a great example; there are other policies internally about disabling default outbound access for subnets (aka, Enable Private Subnet).
One thing I hadn't thought of when submitting this was that my "skip" tags would be captured in the repo and exposed in my module tests; while they aren't secret or anything, it might look weird to external users. How do we feel about that? Would it be worth updating the workflows to pass the tags as part of the workflow rather than hard-coding them into the tests?

comments_list.author: AlexanderSehr
comments_list.body:
Hey @ericscheffler,
we had a conversation about this yesterday and fundamentally agreed to imeplement a solution - with the details still to be figured out.
The corner stones were roughly along the lines of
- Tags should be (optionally) injected by the CI into the test cases
- It should then be possible to pass these tags on into the shared templates (e.g., `dependencies.bicep`) where they would simply be added to all their resources (i.e., the template would have one `param tags object`, keeping the usage rather simple

What we still need to figure out is that injection part for which I want to set up a brainstorming session and collect some ideas to keep it as simple as possible to set up.

comments_list.author: AlexanderSehr
comments_list.body:
Hola @ericscheffler,
wie just had a quick brainstorming sessions and agreed to implement a PoC using the logic that we already have in place (i.e., you could already test it out today). The main points are
- We'd re-use the existing env-specific 'variable/secrets' injection logic ([ref](https://azure.github.io/Azure-Verified-Modules/contributing/bicep/bicep-contribution-flow/custom-ci-secrets/))
- That means, after setting this logic up (which is a key vault + GH variable) one could
   1. Define a secret called e.g., `CI-CustomTags` with a value of `{ "tagA": "valueA", "tagB": "valueB" }`
   2. Define a parameter in the `main.test.bicep` test case like `param customTags string?`
   3. Pass its value to e.g., the `diagnostic.dependencies.bicep` as `tags: json(customTags)` (assuming the `tags` parameter was added to the dependency-template(s) before)
   4. And be in the happy zone

You could even pass the parameter into the `dependencies.bicep` or the main test, even if it has tags hardcoded. For the latter that would look like
```bicep
tags: union(
  {
    'hidden-title': 'This is visible in the resource name'
    Environment: 'Non-Prod'
    Role: 'DeploymentValidation'
  },
  json(tags)
)
``` 

I'll try to test this out in the near future, but cannot commit to a timeline yet with TechConnect upcoming etc. But you should be able to use this already today.

cc: @eriqua , @krbar

comments_list.author: segraef
comments_list.body:
Thanks @ArneRanvik, the schema supports this - `Microsoft.Consumption/budgets` notifications independently carry `operator` + `thresholdType` (`Actual`/`Forecasted`) per notification.

Going additive (non-breaking). Spec for the implementation:

1. In `avm/res/consumption/budget/sub-scope/main.bicep`, add a user-defined type:
   ```bicep
   @export()
   type notificationType = {
     operator: 'EqualTo' | 'GreaterThan' | 'GreaterThanOrEqualTo'
     @minValue(1) @maxValue(1000) threshold: int
     thresholdType: 'Actual' | 'Forecasted'
   }
   ```
2. Add `@maxLength(5) param notifications notificationType[]?` (optional).
3. When `notifications` is non-empty, build `notificationsArray` from it; otherwise fall back to the existing `thresholds` + `thresholdType` (preserves current behaviour - no breaking change).
4. Mark existing `thresholds` and `thresholdType` description with `Deprecated: use 'notifications' for per-threshold control.`
5. Mirror the change in `mg-scope/main.bicep` and `rg-scope/main.bicep`.
6. Update `README.md` (regen via `Set-AVMModule`), and add one test case using the new `notifications` param with mixed `Actual`/`Forecasted`.

Assigning Copilot.

### Check for previous/existing GitHub issues

- [x] I have checked for previous/existing GitHub issues

### Issue Type?

Bug

### Module Name

avm/res/web/site

### (Optional) Module Version

latest

### Description

Description
In the site/config module, when a Storage Account is provided, the module configures four environment variables related to Function App host storage, including:

Storage account name
Blob service URI
Queue service URI
Table service URI

This behavior occurs even when the Function App is configured to use a system-assigned identity for accessing host storage.

Problem Statement
I recently ran into issues related to Function App host storage and reached out to Azure Support. They confirmed that, according to current official Microsoft documentation, when a Function App uses a system-assigned managed identity to connect to host storage, only the storage account name environment variable is required.
The additional service-specific URI environment variables (Blob/Queue/Table) are not required in this scenario and do not appear in Microsoft’s official examples.

Expected Behavior
When a Function App uses a system-assigned identity for host storage access:

Only the storage account name environment variable should be configured.
Explicit service URIs (Blob/Queue/Table) should not be required unless there is a documented requirement.

Aligning the module behavior with official guidance would help avoid unnecessary configuration and potential confusion.

References
Azure Support pointed me to the following official resources:

Microsoft Learn – Connecting to host storage with an identity
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/functions-reference?tabs=blob&pivots=programming-language-csharp#connecting-to-host-storage-with-an-identity

Azure Quickstart Template – Function App (system-assigned identity)
https://github.com/Azure/azure-quickstart-templates/blob/master/quickstarts/microsoft.web/function-app-flex-managed-identities/main.bicep

Both references demonstrate usage where only the storage account name is configured when using a system-assigned identity.

comments_list.body:
Hi @RadicalEddy, thanks for raising this. I’ve taken ownership of the Azure Data Factory AVM module and am currently looking into the issue.
At the moment, the Data Factory AVM module is a thin wrapper that passes the provided `typeProperties` directly to the Linked Service sub-resource (`Microsoft.DataFactory/factories/linkedservices@2018-06-01`) without any transformation or custom logic. Because of that, the module itself does not interpret or modify the `newClusterNumOfWorker` value.
To help isolate where the behavior originates, could you please verify whether the same behavior occurs when you create the Azure Databricks linked service directly (for example, via ARM/Bicep without the AVM module, or through the Azure Portal) using a value like "1:10"?
If autoscaling is still not configured in that scenario, this would indicate a limitation or issue in the Data Factory Linked Service API itself, in which case we should raise this with the product team rather than addressing it in the AVM module.
Thanks for checking, and let me know what you find.

Feature Request

### Module Name

avm/res/network/virtual-network

### (Optional) Module Version

0.7

### Description

The local peering shuold depend on remote.

In scenarios where an environment is repeatedly destroyed and re-created. For example a sandbox used to test IaC and if the environment contains peerings to a network which is outside the destroyed environment (hub network) the remote peering is left in disconnected state. Re-creating the destroyed environment and it's network with peerings fails unless the remote peering is re-created before the local peering. That way the remote peering goes to initiated state and creating the local peering succeeds.

Currently the remote peering doesn't have time to become initated before the local peering is created and ends up in failure.

### (Optional) Correlation Id

_No response_

comments_list.body:
Yes. Here's the module call i make to create the vnet:

```bicep
module vnet 'br/public:avm/res/network/virtual-network:0.7.2' = {
  scope: resourceGroup(vnetCreateInfo.group)
  name: '${deployment().name}-vnet'
  params: {
    name: vnetCreateInfo.name
    addressPrefixes: vnetCreateInfo.addressPrefixes
    subnets: [
      for subnet in vnetCreateInfo.subnets: {
        name: subnet.name
        addressPrefix: subnet.addressPrefix!
        natGatewayResourceId: subnet.?natGatewayResourceId
        networkSecurityGroupResourceId: subnet.?networkSecurityGroupResourceId
        serviceEndpoints: subnet.?serviceEndpoints
        delegation: subnet.?delegation
      }
    ]
    peerings: [
      for peering in vnetCreateInfo.peerings: {
        name: peering.?name
        remotePeeringName: peering.?remotePeeringName
        remotePeeringEnabled: peering.?remotePeeringEnabled
        remoteVirtualNetworkResourceId: peering.remoteVirtualNetworkResourceId
        allowForwardedTraffic: peering.?allowForwardedTraffic
        allowGatewayTransit: peering.?allowGatewayTransit
        allowVirtualNetworkAccess: peering.?allowVirtualNetworkAccess
        doNotVerifyRemoteGateways: peering.?doNotVerifyRemoteGateways
        useRemoteGateways: peering.?useRemoteGateways
        remotePeeringAllowForwardedTraffic: peering.?remotePeeringAllowForwardedTraffic
        remotePeeringAllowGatewayTransit: peering.?remotePeeringAllowGatewayTransit
        remotePeeringAllowVirtualNetworkAccess: peering.?remotePeeringAllowVirtualNetworkAccess
        remotePeeringDoNotVerifyRemoteGateways: peering.?remotePeeringDoNotVerifyRemoteGateways
        remotePeeringUseRemoteGateways: peering.?remotePeeringUseRemoteGateways
      }
    ]
    diagnosticSettings: [
      {
        name: 'logAnalytics'
        workspaceResourceId: analytics.outputs.resourceId 
        logAnalyticsDestinationType: 'Dedicated'
      }
    ]
    enableTelemetry: false
  }
  dependsOn: [ nat ]
}
```
And the parameters showing the peerings: 
```bicep
param vnetCreateInfo = {
  name: 'vnet-sandbox-weu-001'
  group: 'rg-networks-sandbox-weu-001'
  addressPrefixes: ['10.22.32.0/19']
  subnets: [
    { 
      name: 'snet-aks'
      addressPrefix: '10.22.40.0/21'
      natGatewayResourceId: '/subscriptions/f790ae37-59ab-4c20-b54f-xxxxxxxxxxx/resourceGroups/rg-networks-sandbox-weu-001/providers/Microsoft.Network/natGateways/nat-sandbox-weu-001'
      serviceEndpoints: [ 'Microsoft.Sql' ]
    }
    { 
      name: 'snet-api'
      addressPrefix: '10.22.48.0/24'
      delegation: 'Microsoft.Web/serverFarms' 
    }
    {
      name: 'snet-load-balancers'
      addressPrefix: '10.22.49.0/27'
    }
    { 
      name: 'snet-private-endpoints'
      addressPrefix: '10.22.53.0/24'
    }
    { 
      name: 'snet-postgresql'
      addressPrefix: '10.22.55.0/27'
      delegation: 'Microsoft.DBforPostgreSQL/flexibleServers'
    }
  ]
  peerings: [
    {
      name: 'to-vnet-hub-weu-001'
      remotePeeringName: 'to-vnet-sandbox-weu-001'
      remoteVirtualNetworkResourceId: '/subscriptions/2561a685-e167-4a66-8467-xxxxxxxxxxx/resourceGroups/rg-network-hub-weu-001/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/vnet-hub-weu-001'
      remotePeeringEnabled: true
      useRemoteGateways: true
      remotePeeringAllowGatewayTransit: true
      remotePeeringAllowForwardedTraffic: true
    }
  ]
  dnsZoneIds: [
    '/subscriptions/2561a685-e167-4a66-8467-xxxxxxxxxxx/resourceGroups/rg-network-hub-weu-001/providers/Microsoft.Network/privateDnsZones/somedomain.com'
    '/subscriptions/2561a685-e167-4a66-8467-xxxxxxxxxxx/resourceGroups/rg-network-hub-weu-001/providers/Microsoft.Network/privateDnsZones/privatelink.database.windows.net'
  ]
}
```
There's actually nothing special with the module call... It's as basic as it can get and as such there's not really anything wrong.

It's the scenario that raises the probelm. We have vnet setup following the hub and spoke architecture where each spoke is peered to the hub network with the remote peering enabled. The problem raises when we are deploying the sandbox spoke and then later we delete it. Once the spoke network is deleted (peered to hub) the remote peering in the hub network goes to disconnected state. Then when again deploying the sandbox spoke network the peering fails when the existing remote peering in the hub network is in disconnected state.
My suggestion to the vnet module is to depend the local peering from the remote peering.... this way the remote peering is deployed first changing the existing remote peering from disconnected to initiated. Then when the local peering is created it doesn't fail anymore.
Obviously this is not necessary if the peering doesn't exist beforehand, but it doesn't really matter. The only thing is that the remote and local peerings are created in sequence.

### (Optional) Module Version

0.6.0

### Description

This Pattern Module (br/public:avm/ptn/ai-ml/ai-foundry:0.6.0) configures the Foundry with Private endpoints and everything I need to work securely and my access can be set up to use an Azure VPN connection to the Private endpoint. Public access is disabled by default. 
However, the only way to access the "New Foundry Experience" is to enable Public access. I can still have the Private endpoints and they will be used for backend data access, but I need to set up the networking to allow public access so I can use the New Foundry Experience. 
I did not see anything in the AVM documentation about a setting to allow Public Network Access. Specifically, if I were to do this in the UI, I would navigate to the **Azure Foundry Resource> Resource Management> Networking>** and set the **Firewalls and Virtual Networks** tab to **Allow access from: All networks** (All networks, including the internet, can access this resource). 
As soon as I enable this, I can access the New Foundry Experience" in Foundry.
Currently, I cannot set this setting in the Bicep AVM. In modules/account.bicep, the module hardcodes the logic:
`publicNetworkAccess: privateNetworkingEnabled ? 'Disabled' : 'Enabled'`
This means when you configure private endpoints, it automatically sets public access to 'Disabled'. I could like to request the addition of a publicNetworkAccess parameter to aiFoundryConfiguration. This can have a default but allow me to override the value and turn it on, even if I configured Private Endpoints.


### (Optional) Correlation Id

_No response_

comments_list.author: ghost
comments_list.body:
FYI - to work around this issue, I am using the following in my pipeline. The Bicep AVM code will automatically set the Public Access as disabled. This will enable Public Network Access after the Bicep AVM code is complete so that it enabled the "New Foundry Experience".

``` yaml
- task: AzureCLI@2
  displayName: 'Enable Public Access on AI Foundry Account'
  inputs:
    azureSubscription: $(azureResourceManagerConnection)
    scriptType: 'pscore'
    scriptLocation: 'inlineScript'
    inlineScript: |
      $foundryAccountName = 'aifoundryaccount'

      Write-Host "Re-enabling public network access on AI Foundry account: $foundryAccountName"
      az resource update `
        --resource-group $(resourceGroupName) `
        --name $foundryAccountName `
        --resource-type "Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts" `
        --set properties.publicNetworkAccess=Enabled `
        --output none

      if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) {
        Write-Host "Public network access successfully enabled on '$foundryAccountName'."
      }
      else {
        Write-Error "Failed to enable public network access on '$foundryAccountName'."
        exit 1
      }

```

comments_list.author: rickschwabe
comments_list.body:
Thanks for the input and the discussion @fblix and @jtracey93 

My initial thinking was that developers should be able to use the missing capability directly through an AVM module. From a usability perspective it feels natural that subscription placement could be handled natively within AVM rather than requiring users to look for additional patterns.

At the same time, having a clear recommendation for users is important. If the consensus is that this logic should live outside the core modules, then pointing users to the pattern module would make sense as the recommended approach.

So from my perspective: enabling the capability through AVM would be ideal for discoverability and ease of use, but if it remains outside the core modules, the subscription-placement pattern module would be a good candidate to recommend as the standard way to achieve this.

The clarity we added this Pat module as it deployed more than one resource e.g. could move more than one subscription to a specified management group. So I think I’ll recommendation probably should be used the pattern modules either this one or just moving subscriptions to management groups https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/tree/main/avm/ptn/mgmt-groups/subscription-placement

Or the ALZ pattern module if you need to do other things such as create the management group policy assignments, policy definitions et cetera

We felt that if we had it in the resource module and followed the deployed or manage one resource only specification ruling then people having to call a module X number of times to move lots of subscriptions with lead to slow deployment times and also blow the template size eventually where you may need to even have multiple bicep files due to the four megabyte
> 
> So I think I’ll recommendation probably

Hola @jtracey93,
thanks for sharing your thoughts. My only point would be that, given it is a child-resource of the `mgmtGroup` resource provider, technically nothing would speak against implementing and or using it. I agree with you recommendation, but one doesn't need to rule out the other.
One point on the "call it x-number of times": Given that it's a child-resource I believe it's a bit different here. The module deploys 1 mgmt-group instance, but can deploy n-number of it's children (like any other modules), i.e., in this case the subscription placement. It it correct, that each move would create its own deployment, but at least from the management-group module user's perspective, it's a single invocation to move n-amount of subscriptions at once.

issues.body:
### Check for previous/existing GitHub issues

- [x] I have checked for previous/existing GitHub issues

### Issue Type?

Bug

### Module Name

avm/res/web/site

### (Optional) Module Version

0.22.0

### Description

### Summary

When `br/public:avm/res/web/site:0.22.0` is used for Azure Functions Flex Consumption apps, the compiled ARM template still contains the `app_slots` nested deployment subtree even when no slots are configured.

As of March 18, 2026, Microsoft Learn documents that Azure Functions Flex Consumption does not support deployment slots:
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/flex-consumption-plan
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/azure-functions/functions-deployment-slots

### Why this matters

The slot subtree adds a significant amount of unnecessary template payload for Flex Consumption deployments.

In my local build:
- one Function App wrapper includes an `app_slots` subtree of about `163,502` raw bytes / `24,489` gzip bytes
- across four Function Apps, that is about `654,008` raw bytes / `97,956` gzip bytes

This is especially painful in larger Bicep solutions, because it contributes to Azure ARM deployment size limits and can push deployments into `RequestedSizeExceeded` / job size exceeded failures:
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/troubleshooting/error-job-size-exceeded?tabs=bicep

### Actual behavior

Even when:
- no `slots` parameter is passed, or
- `slots: null` is passed explicitly

the generated template still contains the `app_slots` nested deployment definition.

Passing `slots: null` does not remove the subtree. In my case it made the compiled template slightly larger because it only adds an explicit null parameter to the module call.

### Expected behavior

For Azure Functions Flex Consumption:
- slot-related resources/parameters should not be emitted at all, or
- the module should expose a way to fully disable slot generation

Because deployment slots are unsupported for Flex Consumption, emitting the slot deployment subtree provides no runtime value and only increases template size.

### Repro

1. Use `br/public:avm/res/web/site:0.22.0` to deploy an Azure Function App on Flex Consumption.
2. Compile the Bicep template.
3. Inspect the emitted ARM JSON.
4. Observe that `app_slots` is present even though the app does not use slots and Flex Consumption does not support them.

### Requested change

Please consider a Flex-specific code path, or a module switch, that omits slot-related template generation entirely when targeting Flex Consumption.


### (Optional) Correlation Id

c0f34c77-38b0-4927-8855-f38c0fba7ae2

issues.author: chirag1603
issues.body:
### Check for previous/existing GitHub issues

- [x] I have checked for previous/existing GitHub issues

### Issue Type?

Feature Request

### Module Name

avm/res/azure-stack-hci/cluster

### (Optional) Module Version

0.4.0

### Description

## Feature Request: Support Pre-Baked VM Image for E2E Test Infrastructure

### Problem Statement

The `avm/res/azure-stack-hci/cluster` module's e2e deployment tests currently take **5+ hours per test case**, frequently breaching GitHub Actions' **6-hour hard limit**. This causes CI failures unrelated to code quality and blocks PR merges.

Each test run rebuilds the entire nested virtualization environment from scratch — downloading a 3 GB HCI ISO, converting it to VHDX, installing AD DS, DNS, DHCP, Hyper-V roles, and installing Az PowerShell modules (~400 MB) — even though this infrastructure is identical across every run.

### Time Breakdown of Rebuild-from-Scratch Steps

| Step | What's rebuilt every time | Duration |
|------|-------------------------|----------|
| Stage 1 | Install Hyper-V, DNS, DHCP, Clustering roles | ~10 min |
| Stage 3 | Download 3 GB HCI ISO from Microsoft CDN | ~10-15 min |
| Stage 3 | Convert ISO → VHDX (WIM extraction) | ~10 min |
| Stage 3 | Install AD DS Forest (`Install-ADDSForest`) | ~5-10 min |
| Stage 6 | `Install-Module Az` (~400 MB from PSGallery) | ~5-10 min |
| **Total rebuild** | | **~40-55 min per test** |

These steps are **100% deterministic** — same inputs produce same outputs. They could be eliminated by using a pre-baked VM image.

### Proposed Solution

Use a **pre-baked Azure VM image** (via Azure Compute Gallery / Shared Image Gallery) for the host VM instead of starting from a bare Windows Server 2022 image. The pre-baked image would include:

1. **Hyper-V, DNS, DHCP, Clustering roles** — pre-installed
2. **HCI OS VHDX** — pre-cached at a known path (e.g., `C:\ISOs\hci_os.vhdx`)
3. **Az PowerShell modules** — pre-installed
4. **AD DS** — either pre-configured or ready for fast initialization

A working prototype already exists in the repo at:
**`utilities/e2e-template-assets/module-specific/azure-stack-hci/azureStackHCIHost/hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep`**

This file demonstrates the approach using a Shared Image Gallery reference:

```bicep
param imageReferenceId string = '/SharedGalleries/b9e38f20-7c9c-4497-a25d-1a0c5eef2108-DIRECTLYSHARING/Images/vhci-Generalized/Versions/latest'

resource vm 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines@2024-11-01' = {
  properties: {
    storageProfile: {
      imageReference: !empty(imagePublisher)
        ? { publisher: imagePublisher, offer: imageOffer, sku: imageSku, version: imageVersion }
        : { sharedGalleryImageId: imageReferenceId }
    }
  }
}
```

Key improvements in the prototype:
- **Smaller VM size**: Uses `Standard_D16as_v7` instead of `Standard_E32bds_v5` (significant cost reduction)
- **Only 3 runCommands**: `wait` → `ad` (AD provisioning) → `arc1`/`arc2` (Arc onboarding, in parallel) — vs. 8 sequential stages currently
- **No ISO download/conversion**: VHDX pre-baked into the image
- **No role installation**: All roles pre-installed in the image
- **Parallel Arc onboarding**: `arc1` and `arc2` run simultaneously (currently sequential in Stage 6)

### Expected Impact

| Metric | Current | With Pre-Baked Image |
|--------|---------|---------------------|
| Host setup time | ~2.5 hours (Stages 1-7) | ~30-40 min |
| VM size required | Standard_E32bds_v5 (256 GB RAM) | Standard_D16as_v7 (64 GB RAM) |
| Total test time | ~5+ hours | ~2-3 hours |
| CI cost per run | ~$15 (E32bds_v5 × 5h) | ~$3 (D16as_v7 × 2.5h) |
| Stages eliminated | 0 | Stages 1, 3 (partial), 6 (partial) |

### Requirements for Upstream Support

To adopt this approach in the AVM CI pipeline, we need:

1. **Azure Compute Gallery** provisioned in the CI subscription with the pre-baked HCI host image
2. **Image build pipeline** — automated image rebuild when HCI OS version changes (currently `AzureStackHCI23H2.25398.469`)
3. **CI pipeline support** — the `avm-validateModuleDeployment` action and `Test-ModuleLocally.ps1` need to support passing custom image references to test deployments
4. **Shared Image Gallery ID** made available as a CI variable (e.g., `vars.HCI_HOST_IMAGE_ID`)

### Additional Context

- The prototype `hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep` is already functional and has been validated
- The Jumpstart LocalBox project uses a similar pre-baked VHDX approach with `azcopy` from blob storage, confirming this pattern works at scale
- The module is already on the OIDC exception list due to its unique deployment requirements (see related issue for OIDC)
- The HCI e2e test is the **longest-running test in the entire AVM Bicep registry** — no other module comes close to 5+ hours

---

## AVM CI/CD Constraints That Make This Critical

The AVM Bicep framework imposes specific CI/CD requirements that make the current 5+ hour test time untenable. These are not optional — they are **spec-mandated constraints** that the HCI cluster module must operate within.

### Constraint 1: GitHub-Hosted Runners with 6-Hour Hard Limit

AVM Bicep modules run on **`ubuntu-latest` GitHub-hosted runners** ([workflow reference](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/.github/workflows/avm.template.module.yml#L40)). GitHub enforces a **non-configurable 6-hour maximum job duration**. The `avm.template.module.yml` sets `timeout-minutes: 600` but GitHub's own 6-hour hard limit overrides this.

Current HCI cluster tests take **5-6 hours**, leaving zero margin for any variance. Even a 5-minute platform delay can cause a timeout.

### Constraint 2: OIDC Authentication (Federated Credentials)

Per AVM spec, all modules should authenticate via **OIDC (OpenID Connect)** using federated credentials — no long-lived secrets. The HCI cluster module is currently on the [OIDC exception list](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/.github/actions/templates/avm-validateModuleDeployment/action.yml#L101-L110), requiring a service principal + secret. This diverges from the standard and adds operational overhead.

### Constraint 3: Any Subscription / No Pre-Provisioned Resources

AVM e2e tests must be **self-contained** — they create all resources from scratch in a fresh resource group and clean up afterwards. Tests cannot rely on pre-existing resources in the subscription. This is why the test creates the entire nested HCI environment from a bare VM each time.

Relevant code: [avm-validateModuleDeployment/action.yml](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/.github/actions/templates/avm-validateModuleDeployment/action.yml) — the deployment action creates a new RG, deploys, validates, and removes.

### Constraint 4: Mandatory `defaults` and `waf-aligned` Tests

AVM resource modules **must** have both `defaults` and `waf-aligned` e2e test folders ([AVM spec BCPRMNFR1](https://azure.github.io/Azure-Verified-Modules/specs/bcp/res/)). The Pester static validation [enforces this](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/utilities/pipelines/staticValidation/compliance/module.tests.ps1#L314) and blocks `.e2eignore` on these folders for `res/` modules. Both tests run the full 5+ hour deployment.

### Constraint 5: Idempotent Re-Run (Skipped Due to RP Limitation)

AVM tests normally deploy twice to verify idempotency. The HCI module [explicitly skips this](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/avm/res/azure-stack-hci/cluster/tests/e2e/defaults/main.test.bicep#L77) because the `deploymentSettings` RP rejects re-deployment (see [Issue #6776](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/issues/6776)).

## Existing Implementation Already in Repo

This feature request is **not a net-new proposal** — a working pre-baked image deployment path already exists in the repository on \main\ and has been through multiple iterations of stabilization.

### Direct Code References (on \main\)

| File | Purpose | Link |
|------|---------|------|
| \hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep\ | **Pre-baked image host deployment** — uses Shared Image Gallery, only 3 runCommands instead of 8 | [View on main](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/utilities/e2e-template-assets/module-specific/azure-stack-hci/azureStackHCIHost/hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep) |
| \provision-ad.ps1\ | Lightweight AD provisioning script (connects to pre-existing DC VM in the image) | [View on main](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/utilities/e2e-template-assets/module-specific/azure-stack-hci/azureStackHCIHost/scripts/provision-ad.ps1) |
| \provision-arc.ps1\ | Streamlined Arc onboarding (runs per-node, in parallel) | [View on main](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/utilities/e2e-template-assets/module-specific/azure-stack-hci/azureStackHCIHost/scripts/provision-arc.ps1) |
| \wait.ps1\ | Simple parameterized wait script | [View on main](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/utilities/e2e-template-assets/module-specific/azure-stack-hci/azureStackHCIHost/scripts/wait.ps1) |
| \hciHostDeployment.bicep\ | **Current approach** — 8 sequential runCommands building from scratch | [View on main](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/utilities/e2e-template-assets/module-specific/azure-stack-hci/azureStackHCIHost/hciHostDeployment.bicep) |

### Commit History Showing This Was Already Working

| Commit | Description | PR |
|--------|-------------|-----|
| [\975a5e6ef\](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/commit/975a5e6ef) | **\ eat: speed up azlocal test through image packaged (#5189)\** — Original implementation of the pre-baked image approach | [#5189](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/pull/5189) |
| [\d8ebcdadd\](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/commit/d8ebcdadd) | **\ ix: Stablize Nested VM, Use SecureString, Remove Duplicate Installation (#5412)\** — Stabilization of the pre-baked image path | [#5412](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/pull/5412) |
| [\cf22676ac\](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/commit/cf22676ac) | **\ ix: provision arc timeout in azure local (#5208)\** — Timeout fix for Arc provisioning with image | [#5208](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/pull/5208) |
| [\3edc0f44c\](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/commit/3edc0f44c) | **\ ix: add WinRM TrustedHosts config before PSRemoting to nested VMs\** — WinRM fix for image-based deployment | — |

### Key Differences: Image-Based vs Current Approach

| Aspect | \hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep\ (image-based) | \hciHostDeployment.bicep\ (current) |
|--------|--------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| VM Size | \Standard_D16as_v7\ (64 GB) | \Standard_E32bds_v5\ (256 GB) |
| RunCommands | 3 (\wait\ → \d\ → \rc1\/\rc2\ parallel) | 8 (sequential Stages 1-8) |
| Separate disks | None (included in image) | 2× Premium 2TB managed disks |
| NAT Gateway | None (included in image) | Created per deployment |
| ISO download | None (VHDX pre-baked) | 3 GB download + conversion each run |
| AD DS install | Already in image, just provision | \Install-ADDSForest\ from scratch |
| Az modules | Pre-installed in image | \Install-Module Az\ (~400 MB each run) |
| Arc onboarding | **Parallel** (\rc1\ + \rc2\ run simultaneously) | **Sequential** (Stage 6 does both in one job) |
| **Estimated time** | **~30-40 min** | **~2.5-3 hours** |

### What's Needed

The pre-baked image deployment path exists and works. What's needed is:
1. The **Shared Image Gallery image** (\ 9e38f20-7c9c-4497-a25d-1a0c5eef2108\) to be available in the CI subscription
2. The e2e test \dependencies.bicep\ to reference \hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep\ instead of \hciHostDeployment.bicep\
3. An image maintenance pipeline to rebuild when HCI OS versions change

comments_list.author: jtracey93
comments_list.body:
Hi @chirag1603 — thanks for the detailed write-up, this is really well documented and makes the ask clear.

We discussed this on the AVM Bicep weekly sync (2026-04-02) and wanted to come back with our position and a concrete ask.

---

### Our position

We're supportive of using the pre-baked image approach via `hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep` — it already exists, the prototype is validated, and the case for an exception is strong (PG-owned module, similar precedent to SQL modules, 5+ hour test time is untenable).

For injecting the Shared Image Gallery image reference ID into CI, we'd like to use the **AVM Custom CI Secrets** mechanism rather than a bare CI variable — it's the established pattern for tenant-specific values and requires no workflow YAML changes:
👉 https://azure.github.io/Azure-Verified-Modules/contributing/bicep/bicep-contribution-flow/custom-ci-secrets/

The image reference ID would be stored as `CI-hciHostImageReferenceId` in the AVM CI Key Vault, and a matching `@secure() param hciHostImageReferenceId string = ''` in `main.test.bicep` gets automatically populated at test time.

---

### The ask

**We'd like the HCI/Stack PG team to own the Shared Image Gallery and image** rather than AVM — you'll be able to iterate and fix things far faster than routing everything through us, and we don't want to become a blocker on your image lifecycle around new Azure Stack versions etc..

#### 1. Create a Shared Image Gallery + image in your own subscription

You have a working prototype and a validated image already — this is formalising ownership rather than building from scratch.

> ⚠️ The image **must be replicated to `southeastasia`** — that's where AVM CI tests run due to capacity constraints.

#### 2. Share it with the AVM CI subscription

Your preferred option — we're flexible on the mechanism:

- **(a) RBAC on the gallery → AVM CI Managed Identity** *(preferred — most targeted)* — [docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/share-gallery?tabs=portal)
- **(b) Direct shared gallery** *(share with our subscription/tenant, preview feature)* — [docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/share-gallery-direct?tabs=portaldirect)
- **(c) Community gallery** *(fully public — only if no IP concerns)* — [docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/share-gallery-community?tabs=cli)

Once set up, share the image reference ID with us and we'll add `CI-hciHostImageReferenceId` to the AVM CI Key Vault.

#### 3. Own the image maintenance pipeline

Please maintain a process to rebuild/re-capture the image when the HCI OS version changes and notify us to update the secret. We don't want the image version going stale silently.

---

### Code changes (your PR)

Small changes — `hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep` already exists:

- **`main.test.bicep`** (`defaults` + `waf-aligned`): add `@secure() param hciHostImageReferenceId string = ''`, thread into `nestedDependencies`
- **`dependencies.bicep`** (+ `defaults-dependencies.bicep`, `waf-dependencies.bicep`): add param, switch from `hciHostDeployment.bicep` → `hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep`, thread through
- **`hciHostDeploymentWithImage.bicep`**: remove hardcoded `imageReferenceId` default, mark `@secure()`

Include this in your PR description:
```
- [ ] @avm-core-team-technical-bicep TODO: Add custom secret 'CI-hciHostImageReferenceId' to AVM CI Key Vault
```

---

### If hosting isn't possible on your side

Let us know — we can host the gallery on the AVM side and grant your team maintainer access so you still own the image lifecycle. We'd strongly prefer you own it, but we don't want it to be a blocker.

---

📖 Further reading:
- [AVM Custom CI Secrets](https://azure.github.io/Azure-Verified-Modules/contributing/bicep/bicep-contribution-flow/custom-ci-secrets/)
- [AVM Bicep contribution flow](https://azure.github.io/Azure-Verified-Modules/contributing/bicep/bicep-contribution-flow/)
- [Azure Compute Gallery sharing options](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/share-gallery?tabs=portal)

### Check for previous/existing GitHub issues

### Issue Type?

Bug

### Module Name

avm/res/azure-stack-hci/cluster

### (Optional) Module Version

0.4.0

### Description

## Bug: Azure Stack HCI Cluster Module Requires OIDC Exception and Has Non-Idempotent deploymentSettings

### Summary

The `avm/res/azure-stack-hci/cluster` module has two interrelated CI/CD issues:

1. **OIDC Exception**: The module is currently on the OIDC exception list, requiring service principal + secret authentication instead of the standard OIDC flow used by all other AVM modules
2. **Non-Idempotent `deploymentSettings`**: The `Microsoft.AzureStackHCI/clusters/deploymentSettings` resource does not support idempotent re-deployment. Once it enters `DeploymentFailed` state, no further operations are allowed — the only recovery is to delete the entire cluster resource and start over

### Issue 1: OIDC Exception

The module is listed in the [OIDC exception list](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/blob/main/.github/actions/templates/avm-validateModuleDeployment/action.yml) in the deployment validation action:

```yaml
$exceptionModulePaths = @(
    'avm/res/azure-stack-hci/cluster'    # Failing on resource deletion when trying to delete RBAC at subscription level
    'avm/res/azure-stack-hci/logical-network'
    'avm/res/azure-stack-hci/network-interface'
    'avm/res/azure-stack-hci/virtual-hard-disk'
    'avm/res/azure-stack-hci/virtual-machine-instance'
    ...
)
```

**Root cause**: The module creates subscription-level role assignments during deployment (Contributor, Reader, RBAC Admin). During cleanup, the OIDC-based identity may lack permissions to delete these subscription-scoped assignments, causing the removal step to fail and leaving orphaned resources.

**Impact**: Requires maintaining a service principal with secret rotation, adds operational overhead, and diverges from the standard AVM CI authentication pattern.


### Requested Changes

#### For OIDC Exception
1. Investigate why OIDC-authenticated identities fail on subscription-level RBAC cleanup for HCI modules


### Environment

- Azure region: `southeastasia`
- API version: `2025-10-01` (`Microsoft.AzureStackHCI/clusters/deploymentSettings`)
- Module version: `0.4.0`
- Host VM: `Standard_E32bds_v5` with 2-node nested HCI cluster
- HCI OS: `AzureStackHCI23H2.25398.469`

PR [#4393](vscode-file://vscode-app/c:/Users/chchoudha/AppData/Local/Programs/Microsoft%20VS%20Code/072586267e/resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html) (Feb 10, 2025) by Erika Gressi (AVM core team member) added the OIDC exception for [cluster](vscode-file://vscode-app/c:/Users/chchoudha/AppData/Local/Programs/Microsoft%20VS%20Code/072586267e/resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html). The commit message states:

"hub-spoke test is failing on role assignment removal when leveraging OIDC. Adding it back to the exception list to fall back to SP+secret authentication method, while the issue is being troubleshooted. Same issue with the yet-to-be-published [cluster](vscode-file://vscode-app/c:/Users/chchoudha/AppData/Local/Programs/Microsoft%20VS%20Code/072586267e/resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html) module tests"

SP+secret has broader permissions that allow this cleanup.

The other 4 HCI modules were added by xhy8759 (Hang Xu, the original HCI module author) and Erika as they were published — each module creates similar subscription-level RBAC and hits the same cleanup issue:

issues.author: ilazarev
issues.body:
### Module path

avm/ptn/ai-ml/ai-foundry

### Module version

`0.6.0`

### Summary

Preview flows fail before a what-if result is produced when the AI Foundry pattern creates internal associated-resource RBAC assignments from principal IDs that are only materialized later in the same deployment.

In our repo this shows up through both:

- `azd provision --preview`
- `az deployment sub what-if --validation-level Template`

The raw preview path fails with:

```text
InvalidTemplate: The provided value for the template parameter 'roleAssignments[0]' is not valid. A non-null value for the property 'principalId' must be provided, but the property was null or missing.
```

### Repro shape

The repro uses the AI Foundry pattern with associated resources enabled, including AI Search and Storage, so the module synthesizes RBAC for those resources and for the created project.

### Compiled template evidence

From the compiled ARM output generated from the module usage:

- the storage associated-resource deployment builds `roleAssignments` by concatenating user-provided assignments with new entries whose `principalId` values come from `reference('foundryAccount').outputs.systemAssignedMIPrincipalId.value` and `reference('aiSearch').outputs.systemAssignedMIPrincipalId.value`
- the project-related RBAC deployments pass `reference('project', '2025-07-01-preview', 'full').identity.principalId` into nested role-assignment deployments

Those same-deployment identity references are valid for real deployment ordering, but preview validation appears to evaluate them too early.

### Why this seems module-related

We already moved some repo-local RBAC assignments outside the AI Foundry module to reduce preview failures, but the remaining failure still comes from the module's internal associated-resource/project RBAC generation.

### Expected behavior

The module should remain previewable in ARM what-if / `azd provision --preview`, even if the actual role assignments are created later in the deployment.

### Actual behavior

Preview fails during template validation and produces no usable diff unless the caller strips the preview-hostile RBAC sections from a temporary compiled template.

### Suggested fix directions

1. Avoid constructing preview-critical `roleAssignments` arrays from same-deployment managed-identity outputs inside the main pattern path.
2. Split those associated-resource RBAC deployments into a phase that can be disabled or deferred for preview-sensitive scenarios.
3. Expose an option to skip/defer internal associated-resource RBAC and project-connection RBAC so callers can keep preview working without forking the module.
4. Where possible, prefer existing-resource lookups for already-deployed resources instead of preview-time references to fresh outputs.

### Environment

- `azd 1.23.15`
- `azure-cli 2.84.0`
- preview attempted at subscription scope

If helpful, I can provide a minimized repro that isolates just the AI Foundry pattern and the failing associated-resource RBAC path.

Cannot create networks without peering to the vWAN hub in subscription vending when the network is defined under additional networks.

### Issue Type?

Bug

### Module Name

avm/ptn/mgmt-groups/subscription-placement

### (Optional) Module Version

0.3.0

### Description

Subscriptions are never moved to their target management groups when using the default parameters. The compiled ARM template contains an inverted condition on the placement resource. It only executes when disableSubscriptionPlacement is true, which is the opposite of the intended behaviour.

**Steps to reproduce**

Deploy avm/ptn/mgmt-groups/subscription-placement:0.3.0 with a standard parSubscriptionPlacement array (no disableSubscriptionPlacement field set).

Observe that no Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/subscriptions resources are created and subscriptions remain in their original management group.

**Workaround**

Set disableSubscriptionPlacement: true on every entry in parSubscriptionPlacement. This exploits the inverted condition to actually trigger placement.

**Expected behaviour**

Subscriptions are placed when disableSubscriptionPlacement is omitted or false. Setting disableSubscriptionPlacement: true should skip placement for that entry.

### (Optional) Correlation Id

_No response_

comments_list.author: tauzN
comments_list.body:
Current implementation (buggy)

```
...
for (subscriptionPlacement, index) in parSubscriptionPlacement: if (subscriptionPlacement.?disableSubscriptionPlacement == true) {
...
```

The condition needs to be negated so placement runs by default and is skipped only when the flag is explicitly set to true:


Proposed fix

```
...
for (subscriptionPlacement, index) in parSubscriptionPlacement: if (!(subscriptionPlacement.?disableSubscriptionPlacement ?? false)) {
...
```

The ?? false handles the nullable case (field omitted); without it, !(null) would error. This way:


| disableSubscriptionPlacement | condition evaluates to | result |
|--------|--------|--------|
| omitted | !(null ?? false) = !false = true | placement runs |
| false | !(false) = true | placement runs |
| true | !(true) = false | placement skipped |

issues.author: chirag1603
issues.body:
### Check for previous/existing GitHub issues

- I have checked for previous/existing GitHub issues

### Issue Type?

Bug/Feature Request (Hybrid)

### Module Name

All Azure Stack HCI edge modules:
- `avm/res/azure-stack-hci/virtual-machine-instance`
- `avm/res/azure-stack-hci/logical-network`
- `avm/res/azure-stack-hci/marketplace-gallery-image`
- `avm/res/azure-stack-hci/cluster`

### Description

## Problem Statement

All Azure Stack HCI modules that deploy resources **on top of an HCI cluster** (VMI, logical-network, marketplace-gallery-image) consistently run **5h 30min – 5h 55min** in E2E deployment validation, frequently breaching the **6-hour GitHub Actions hard limit**. This causes CI failures completely unrelated to code quality and blocks PR merges.

Unlike the cluster module itself (tracked in #6775), these "edge" modules have an **additional deployment layer** — they must first create the full HCI cluster infrastructure, then deploy their module under test, then clean up. This makes them **even more time-constrained** than the cluster module alone.

---

## Detailed Timing Analysis (VMI Module — Representative Example)

**Successful run**: [#24930356710](https://github.com/chirag1603/bicep-registry-modules/actions/runs/24930356710) — **5h 54min** (6 min from timeout)

### Phase-by-Phase Breakdown

| Phase | Start (UTC) | End (UTC) | Duration | % of Total |
|-------|-------------|-----------|----------|------------|
| Job setup + checkout | 11:59 | 12:04 | ~5 min | 1% |
| **Host VM deployment** | 12:04 | 12:51 | **~47 min** | 13% |
| **HCI cluster validation (56 steps)** | 12:51 | 13:54 | **~63 min** | 18% |
| **HCI cluster deployment (56 steps)** | 13:54 | 16:27 | **~153 min** | 44% |
| Marketplace image provisioning | 16:27 | 16:58 | ~31 min | 9% |
| **VMI deployment (module under test)** | 16:58 | 17:31 | **~33 min** | 9% |
| Resource cleanup (52 resources) | 17:31 | 17:52 | ~21 min | 6% |
| **Total** | | | **~5h 53min** | 100% |

### Key Observation

The **module under test (VMI) only takes ~33 minutes** (9% of total time). The remaining **91% is shared infrastructure** — host VM, HCI cluster creation, and cleanup. This ratio is similar for all HCI edge modules:

| Module | Module Deploy Time | Total E2E Time | Infrastructure Overhead |
|--------|-------------------|----------------|------------------------|
| VMI | ~33 min | ~5h 54min | 91% |
| Logical-network | ~5 min | ~5h 30min | 98% |
| Marketplace-gallery-image | ~30 min | ~5h 40min | 91% |
| Cluster (standalone) | N/A | ~5h 20min | 100% (is the infra) |

---

## Cleanup Phase Detail

The AVM pipeline removes resources **one-by-one** in priority order (not RG-level delete). For HCI modules, this means removing 52 resources individually:

| Cleanup Step | Duration | Bottleneck |
|-------------|----------|------------|
| Role assignments (11) | ~1.5 min | — |
| Diagnostic settings | ~10 sec | — |
| **KeyVault delete + soft-delete purge** | **~10 min** | **Biggest bottleneck** |
| Virtual Machine | ~2 min | — |
| MSIs + Resource Group | ~15 sec | — |
| Post-cleanup overhead | ~7 min | — |
| **Total** | **~21 min** | |

**Optimization applied**: We've set `enableSoftDelete: false` on the test KeyVault (following the pattern used by `avm/res/network/application-gateway` and `avm/res/web/serverfarm`). This eliminates the ~10 min purge wait. PR forthcoming.

---

## Why This Affects All HCI Edge Modules

Every HCI module that runs on an HCI cluster shares the same test dependency chain:

```
main.test.bicep
  └── dependencies.bicep (shared test harness)
        ├── hciHostDeployment.bicep    → Azure VM with nested Hyper-V (~47 min)
        │   ├── Stage 1-2: Install features + reboot
        │   ├── Stage 3-4: VHDX/AD/networking + reboot  
        │   └── Stage 5: DHCP + Hyper-V switches + Arc connection
        ├── ashciPrereqs.bicep         → KeyVault, storage, secrets (~5 min)
        └── HCI Cluster resource       → Cluster shell (~1 min)
  └── cluster module (br/public:avm/res/azure-stack-hci/cluster:0.4.0)
        └── ECE Validate + Deploy      → 56 steps (~3.5 hours)
  └── Module under test                → Actual test (~5-33 min)
  └── Cleanup                          → 52 resources (~21 min)
```

**~5 hours of this pipeline is identical across all modules.** Only the last 5-33 minutes differ.

---

## AVM CI/CD Constraints That Make This Critical

| Constraint | AVM Spec | Impact on HCI |
|-----------|----------|---------------|
| **6-hour hard limit** | GitHub-hosted runners (`ubuntu-latest`) | Zero margin at 5h54m |
| **Self-contained tests** | No pre-provisioned resources | Must rebuild entire HCI env from scratch |
| **Mandatory defaults + waf-aligned** | BCPRMNFR1 | 2× full deployments per PR |
| **Resource cleanup required** | `removeDeployment: true` | 21 min cleanup per test case |
| **vCPU quota** | Shared subscription (100 cores) | E48 host = max 2 parallel tests |

---

## Proposed Solutions (for Core Team Discussion)

### Short-term (within current framework)

1. **✅ KeyVault soft-delete disabled** — saves ~10 min per test (PR in progress)
2. **Increase job timeout** — if self-hosted runners or larger runners are available
3. **Sequential test execution** — run defaults first, cleanup, then waf-aligned (avoids quota issues)

### Medium-term (requires core team support)

4. **Pre-baked VM image** (detailed in #6775) — eliminates ~40-55 min of host setup per run
5. **Shared cluster infrastructure** — deploy HCI cluster once, run multiple module tests against it, then cleanup
6. **Parallel cleanup** — remove resources in parallel instead of sequentially where safe

### Long-term (architectural)

7. **Persistent test environment** — maintain a standing HCI cluster for validation (similar to how some Azure services maintain test beds)
8. **Split validation** — static validation + PSRule in one job, deployment in a separate longer-running job with extended timeout

---

## Evidence: Upstream CI Also Failing

The upstream CI run triggered by the VMI PR merge is also hitting this timeout:

- **Run**: [#24949247881](https://github.com/Azure/bicep-registry-modules/actions/runs/24949247881) — both deploy jobs cancelled (still running after 6+ hours)
- This confirms the issue affects the **upstream Azure/bicep-registry-modules** CI, not just fork runs

---

## Related Issues

- #6775 — HCI cluster module pre-baked image proposal (addresses host setup time)
- #6776 — HCI cluster deployment idempotency limitation

### Additional Context

All timing data collected from actual CI runs on the fork `chirag1603/bicep-registry-modules` with `Standard_E48bds_v5` host VMs (48 vCPU, 384GB RAM) in `southeastasia` region. The 6-hour limit is a hard constraint of GitHub Actions that cannot be configured.

comments_list.author: chirag1603
comments_list.body:
## 🏗️ Recommendation: Dedicated/Self-Hosted GitHub Runners for HCI Edge Modules

After reviewing the detailed timing analysis in this issue and researching the available options, it's clear that the **6-hour GitHub Actions hard limit is fundamentally incompatible** with HCI edge module E2E validation. Below is a comprehensive analysis of runner options and a concrete proposal.

---

### 1. Why GitHub-Hosted Runners Cannot Work for HCI Edge Modules

| Constraint | GitHub-Hosted Runner Limit | HCI Edge Reality |
|---|---|---|
| **Job timeout** | **6 hours (360 min) — hard limit, not configurable** | Tests consistently run **5h30m–5h55m** |
| **Remaining margin** | N/A | **5–30 minutes** (effectively zero) |
| **Timeout extension** | ❌ Not possible | Any Azure deployment slowdown = CI failure |
| **Runner persistence** | Ephemeral (clean VM each run) | No dependency caching possible |

> **Key fact**: GitHub-hosted runners enforce a **hard 6-hour per-job timeout** that [cannot be extended](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/administering-github-actions/usage-limits-billing-and-administration). This is a platform-level constraint, not a workflow configuration. Self-hosted runners have **no such limit** by default.

Any small regression in Azure RP deployment time (which is outside our control) immediately causes CI failures **completely unrelated to code quality**. This is the core problem.

---

### 2. Option A: Self-Hosted GitHub Runners (Recommended)

Self-hosted runners provide full control over timeout, hardware, and environment. Key benefits for HCI:

| Benefit | Impact on HCI E2E Tests |
|---|---|
| **No 6-hour timeout** | Can set `timeout-minutes: 480` (8h) or `600` (10h) for safety margin |
| **Regional co-location** | Deploy runner in `southeastasia` (same region as HCI test infra) → lower API latency |
| **Dependency pre-caching** | Pre-install Bicep CLI, Az modules, test tooling → save ~5 min per run |
| **Persistent storage** | Cache large VHDX downloads and VM images across runs |
| **Warm Azure connection** | Maintain authenticated session, reducing auth overhead |
| **Custom hardware** | Match or exceed the `Standard_E48bds_v5` test VM requirements |

#### Proposed Workflow Configuration

```yaml
jobs:
  e2e-hci-edge:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, hci-edge]
    timeout-minutes: 480  # 8 hours — provides ~2h margin over current ~5h55m
    env:
      AZURE_REGION: southeastasia
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      # ... existing E2E test steps
```

#### Runner Labels

| Label | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `self-hosted` | Required base label for self-hosted runners |
| `hci-edge` | Custom label to route only HCI edge module jobs to these runners |
| `linux` | OS label (Ubuntu-based runner) |

#### Security Considerations (Critical for Public Repo)

Since `Azure/bicep-registry-modules` is a **public repository**, self-hosted runners require careful security hardening:

1. **Use ephemeral runners** — destroy and recreate the runner VM after each job using [actions-runner-controller (ARC)](https://github.com/actions/actions-runner-controller) or similar
2. **Restrict to specific workflows** — only route HCI edge module workflows to self-hosted runners; all other modules continue using GitHub-hosted runners
3. **Network isolation** — place runners in a locked-down VNet with only required outbound access (Azure APIs, GitHub)
4. **No secrets on runner** — use OIDC federation or just-in-time secret injection, never persist credentials on the runner
5. **Require approval for fork PRs** — ensure `pull_request_target` or manual approval gates prevent untrusted fork code from running on self-hosted runners
6. **Regular patching** — automated OS and runner software updates

> **Reference**: [GitHub Docs — Security hardening for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions)

---

### 3. Option B: GitHub Larger Runners

GitHub now offers ["larger runners"](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-github-hosted-runners/about-larger-runners) with significantly more compute (up to 96 vCPU, 384 GB RAM). However:

| Aspect | Larger Runners | Self-Hosted Runners |
|---|---|---|
| **Timeout** | ⚠️ **Still 6-hour hard limit** | ✅ No limit (configurable) |
| **Compute** | Up to 96 vCPU / 384 GB RAM | Custom (your choice) |
| **Regional control** | Limited regions | ✅ Any Azure region |
| **Dependency caching** | Ephemeral (no persistence) | ✅ Persistent |
| **Cost** | Per-minute billing | Fixed VM cost |
| **Availability** | GitHub Team/Enterprise plans only | Any plan |

**Verdict**: Larger runners could speed up non-deployment phases (checkout, template compilation, validation) but **do not solve the timeout problem**. They may shave 5–10 minutes off the total, but the ~5h of Azure infrastructure deployment is the bottleneck, not runner compute power. Larger runners are a complement, not a solution.

> **Reference**: [GitHub Docs — About larger runners](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-github-hosted-runners/about-larger-runners/about-larger-runners)

---

### 4. Option C: Azure DevOps Pipelines (Alternative)

If self-hosted GitHub runners are not feasible, **Azure DevOps Pipelines** offer significantly more flexibility:

| Feature | GitHub Actions (Hosted) | Azure DevOps (Self-Hosted Agent) |
|---|---|---|
| **Max job timeout** | 6 hours (hard limit) | **48 hours** (configurable via `timeoutInMinutes: 2880`) |
| **Agent persistence** | Ephemeral | Persistent or ephemeral |
| **Regional deployment** | Limited | Any Azure region |
| **Integration** | Native to GitHub | Requires repo sync or trigger |

```yaml
# Azure DevOps Pipeline example
jobs:
- job: HCI_E2E_Validation
  timeoutInMinutes: 480  # 8 hours
  pool:
    name: HCI-SelfHosted-Pool
  steps:
    # ... test steps
```

> **Reference**: [Azure DevOps Docs — Job timeout](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/process/phases?view=azure-devops&tabs=yaml#timeouts)

---

### 5. Impact Analysis

This is not a one-module problem. **Every current and future HCI edge module** is affected:

| Module | Current Status | E2E Time | Timeout Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `azure-stack-hci/virtual-machine-instance` | Published | ~5h 54min | 🔴 Critical (6 min margin) |
| `azure-stack-hci/logical-network` | In Development | ~5h 30min | 🟡 High (30 min margin) |
| `azure-stack-hci/marketplace-gallery-image` | In Development | ~5h 40min | 🟡 High (20 min margin) |
| `azure-stack-hci/cluster` | Published | ~5h 20min | 🟡 High (40 min margin) |
| `azure-stack-hci/storage-path` | Planned | ~5h 30min (est.) | 🟡 High |
| `azure-stack-hci/virtual-hard-disk` | Planned | ~5h 35min (est.) | 🟡 High |
| `azure-stack-hci/network-interface` | Planned | ~5h 30min (est.) | 🟡 High |

**~91–98% of each module's E2E time is shared infrastructure overhead.** As more HCI edge modules are added, this problem scales linearly — each new module faces the same timeout cliff.

---

### 6. Cost-Benefit Analysis

| Factor | Current State (GitHub-Hosted) | With Self-Hosted Runner |
|---|---|---|
| **Runner cost** | Included in GitHub plan | ~$150–300/month for a `Standard_D4s_v5` Azure VM (4 vCPU, 16 GB) |
| **CI failure rate (timeout)** | ~20–30% of runs fail due to timeout | ~0% timeout failures |
| **Developer time wasted** | ~2–4 hours per timeout failure (investigate, re-trigger, wait) | Minimal |
| **PR merge delay** | 1–3 days due to retry cycles | Same-day merges |
| **Retry cost** | Each retry = another 6h of GitHub Actions minutes | Reduced retries |
| **Opportunity cost** | Blocks HCI module development velocity | Unblocks pipeline |

**Conservative estimate**: At 2 timeout failures/week × 3 hours developer time × $75/hr loaded cost = **~$450/week in wasted developer time**. A self-hosted runner at ~$200/month pays for itself within the first week.

---

### 7. Proposed Action Plan

| Priority | Action | Owner | Timeline |
|---|---|---|---|
| P0 | ✅ Apply KeyVault soft-delete optimization (saves ~10 min) | Module owners | Immediate (PR in progress) |
| P1 | Evaluate self-hosted runner feasibility for HCI modules | AVM Core Team | 2–4 weeks |
| P1 | Define security requirements for self-hosted runners in public repo | AVM Core Team + Security | 2–4 weeks |
| P2 | Pilot self-hosted runner with `hci-edge` label for VMI module | Infra Team | 4–6 weeks |
| P2 | Implement pre-baked VM image (#6775) in parallel | Module owners | 4–8 weeks |
| P3 | Roll out to all HCI edge module workflows | AVM Core Team | 6–10 weeks |

---

### 8. Official Documentation References

- **Self-hosted runners**: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/hosting-your-own-runners/managing-self-hosted-runners/about-self-hosted-runners
- **Larger runners**: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-github-hosted-runners/about-larger-runners/about-larger-runners
- **GitHub Actions usage limits**: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/administering-github-actions/usage-limits-billing-and-administration
- **Security hardening**: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions
- **Actions Runner Controller (ARC)**: https://github.com/actions/actions-runner-controller
- **Azure DevOps job timeout**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/process/phases?view=azure-devops&tabs=yaml#timeouts

---

**TL;DR**: The 6-hour GitHub Actions hard limit is a **structural blocker** for all HCI edge modules. Self-hosted runners with an `[self-hosted, hci-edge]` label and `timeout-minutes: 480` is the most straightforward fix. This should be combined with the pre-baked image work in #6775 to reduce the overall E2E time. Larger runners alone won't solve this since the bottleneck is Azure deployment time, not runner compute. The cost of a self-hosted runner (~$200/month) is trivial compared to the developer time currently wasted on timeout-related CI failures.

issues.body:
### Check for previous/existing GitHub issues

- [x] I have checked for previous/existing GitHub issues

### Issue Type?

Feature Request

### Module Name

avm/res/network/bastion-host

### (Optional) Module Version

0.8.2

### Description

# Issue Summary

The AVM module `avm/res/network/bastion-host` (latest: v0.8.2, API version `2025-01-01`) exposes `enableSessionRecording: bool` but does **not** expose any parameter for configuring the session recording storage backend. Setting `enableSessionRecording: true` without a configured storage target renders the Bastion Host non-functional — all RDP/SSH connections fail with:

> **"Cannot connect to session without valid SAS URL"**

This is a critical usability gap: the module allows enabling a feature that requires additional configuration it cannot provide, resulting in a broken Bastion deployment with no portal-visible error until a user attempts to connect.

## Affected Module

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Module | `br/public:avm/res/network/bastion-host` |
| Current version | `0.8.2` |
| API version (module) | `2025-01-01` |
| Latest ARM API version | `2025-05-01` |
| GitHub repo | `Azure/bicep-registry-modules` |
| Module path | `avm/res/network/bastion-host` |
| Issue type | Feature Request |

## Root Cause Analysis

### What the module does today

The module's `main.bicep` constructs the `bastionpropertiesVar` object and sets `enableSessionRecording` for Premium SKU:

```bicep
(skuName == 'Premium'
  ? {
      enableSessionRecording: enableSessionRecording
      enablePrivateOnlyBastion: enablePrivateOnlyBastion
    }
  : {})
```

It also has tunneling-interaction logic:

```bicep
enableTunneling: skuName == 'Standard' ? true : (enableSessionRecording ? false : true)
```

### What the module does NOT do

The module does not set either of the two properties required by the Azure Bastion resource provider for session recording to function:

1. **`storageContainersSasUrls`** — an array of SAS URLs pointing to the blob container for session recordings (legacy method)
2. **Session Recording Configuration with Managed Identity** — the recommended (preview) approach using system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity with a blob container URI

Neither property is parameterised, passed through, or documented as a prerequisite.

### What happens at runtime

1. ARM deploys the Bastion with `enableSessionRecording: true` — deployment **succeeds** (no validation error)
2. Tunneling is auto-disabled (`enableTunneling: false`) — native client (`az network bastion rdp/ssh`) stops working
3. Any RDP/SSH connection attempt via the portal fails with the SAS URL error
4. The Bastion is effectively non-functional until session recording is disabled or a storage target is configured via the portal/REST API

### Additional complication

`Set-AzBastion` cannot be used to fix the issue because it drops availability zones on update, causing error `BastionHostZonesCannotBeModified` (400). The only reliable fix is a GET-modify-PUT via `Invoke-AzRestMethod`, or manual portal configuration.

## Impact

| Impact | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Connectivity loss | All RDP/SSH sessions fail until storage is configured or session recording is disabled |
| Tunneling disabled | Native client support (`az network bastion rdp/ssh`) is auto-disabled when session recording is enabled |
| No deployment-time validation | ARM accepts the deployment without error; failure is only visible at connection time |
| No IaC workaround | Consumers cannot configure storage via Bicep — must use portal, REST API, or PowerShell post-deployment |

## Evidence

### Environment

- **Bastion resource:** `ahc-pcon-bas-msp-prd-uks-001`
- **Resource group:** `ahc-pcon-rg-msp-prd-uks-043`
- **Subscription:** Connectivity Production (`b18df9fc-0108-462b-bd36-9a0cf9666e1f`)
- **SKU:** Premium, Zones: [1, 2, 3], Location: UK South

### Reproduction steps

1. Deploy Bastion using AVM module with `enableSessionRecording: true`
2. Deployment completes successfully (provisioning state: Succeeded)
3. Attempt to connect to any VM via portal RDP/SSH
4. Connection fails: "Cannot connect to session without valid SAS URL"

### Resolution applied (manual)

Session recording was disabled via direct REST API call:

```powershell
# GET current state
$bastion = Invoke-AzRestMethod -Path "/subscriptions/{subId}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/Microsoft.Network/bastionHosts/{name}?api-version=2024-05-01" -Method GET

# Modify properties
$body = $bastion.Content | ConvertFrom-Json
$body.properties.enableSessionRecording = $false
$body.properties.enableTunneling = $true

# PUT back
Invoke-AzRestMethod -Path "/subscriptions/{subId}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/Microsoft.Network/bastionHosts/{name}?api-version=2024-05-01" -Method PUT -Payload ($body | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20)
```

---

## Requested Changes to AVM Module

### Option A — Managed Identity Support (Recommended)

Add parameters to support the managed identity approach (now recommended by Microsoft):

```bicep
@description('Optional. Enable system-assigned managed identity for session recording storage access.')
param enableSystemAssignedIdentity bool = false

@description('Optional. Blob container URI for session recording storage (e.g. https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<container>).')
param sessionRecordingBlobContainerUri string = ''
```

The module should:

- Enable system-assigned managed identity on the Bastion resource when `enableSessionAssignedIdentity: true`
- Configure the session recording blob container URI
- Validate that `sessionRecordingBlobContainerUri` is non-empty when `enableSessionRecording` is true
- Optionally assign `Storage Blob Data Contributor` role on the storage account

### Option B — SAS URL Support (Legacy)

Add a parameter for SAS URL configuration:

```bicep
@description('Optional. Array of SAS URLs for session recording storage containers.')
param storageContainersSasUrls string[] = []
```

The module should pass this through to the `bastionpropertiesVar` object.

### Option C — Validation Guard (Minimum)

At minimum, add a compile-time validation that prevents enabling session recording without storage configuration:

```bicep
assert sessionRecordingRequiresStorage = !enableSessionRecording || !empty(storageContainersSasUrls) || !empty(sessionRecordingBlobContainerUri)
```

### Additional considerations

- The `enableTunneling` logic already accounts for session recording — no changes needed there
- Documentation should explicitly warn that enabling session recording without storage configuration will break connectivity
- E2E tests should include a Premium SKU test case with session recording enabled and storage configured

---


### (Optional) Correlation Id

_No response_
